{{Short description|Pathological topological space}}
In mathematics, particularly [[topology]], a '''comb space''' is a particular [[subspace topology|subspace]] of <math>\R^2</math> that resembles a [[comb]]. The comb space has properties that serve as a number of [[counterexamples]]. The [[topologist's sine curve]] has similar properties to the comb space.  The '''deleted comb space''' is a variation on the comb space.
[[File:Comb.svg|right|thumb|Topologist's comb]]
[[File:Double comb.svg|right|thumb|The intricated double comb for r=3/4.]]

==Formal definition==

Consider <math>\R^2</math> with its [[standard topology]] and let ''K'' be the [[Set (mathematics)|set]] <math>\{1/n ~|~ n \in \mathbb N\}</math>. The set ''C'' defined by:

:<math>(\{0\} \times [0,1] ) \cup (K \times [0,1]) \cup ([0,1] \times \{0\})</math>

considered as a subspace of <math>\R^2</math> equipped with the [[subspace topology]] is known as the comb space. The deleted comb space, D, is defined by:

:<math>(\{0\} \times \{1 \}) \cup (K \times [0,1]) \cup ([0,1] \times \{0\})   </math>.

This is the comb space with the line segment <math>\{0\} \times (0,1)</math> deleted.

==Topological properties==

The comb space and the deleted comb space have some interesting topological properties mostly related to the notion of [[locally connected space|connectedness]].

* The comb space, C, is path connected and [[Contractible space|contractible]], but not locally contractible, [[Locally connected space|locally path connected]], or locally connected.
* The deleted comb space, D, is connected:
*:Let E be the comb space without <math>\{0\} \times (0,1] </math>.  E is also path connected and the [[Closure (topology)|closure]] of E is the comb space. As E <math>\subset</math> D <math>\subset</math> the closure of E, where E is connected, the deleted comb space is also connected.
*The deleted comb space is not path connected since there is no [[Path (topology)|path]] from (0,1) to (0,0):
*:Suppose there is a path from ''p'' = (0,&nbsp;1) to the point (0,&nbsp;0) in ''D''. Let ''f''&nbsp;:&nbsp;[0,&nbsp;1]&nbsp;→&nbsp;''D'' be this path. We shall prove that ''f''<sup>&nbsp;&minus;1</sup>{''p''} is both [[Open set|open]] and [[Closed set|closed]] in [0,&nbsp;1] contradicting the [[connected space|connectedness]] of this set. Clearly we have ''f''<sup>&nbsp;&minus;1</sup>{''p''} is closed in [0,&nbsp;1] by the [[Continuous function|continuity]] of ''f''. To prove that ''f''<sup>&nbsp;&minus;1</sup>{''p''} is open, we proceed as follows: Choose a [[Neighbourhood (mathematics)|neighbourhood]] ''V'' (open in '''R'''<sup>2</sup>) about ''p'' that doesn't intersect the ''x''–axis. Suppose ''x'' is an arbitrary point in ''f''<sup>&nbsp;&minus;1</sup>{''p''}. Clearly, ''f''(''x'') = ''p''. Then since ''f''<sup>&nbsp;&minus;1</sup>(''V'') is open, there is a [[basis (topology)|basis]] element ''U'' containing ''x'' such that ''f''(''U'') is a subset of ''V''.  We assert that ''f''(''U'') = {''p''} which will mean that ''U'' is an open subset of ''f''<sup>&nbsp;&minus;1</sup>{''p''} containing ''x''. Since ''x'' was arbitrary, ''f''<sup>&nbsp;&minus;1</sup>{''p''} will then be open. We know that ''U'' is connected since it is a basis element for the [[order topology]] on [0,&nbsp;1]. Therefore, ''f''(''U'') is connected. Suppose ''f''(''U'') contains a point ''s'' other than ''p''.  Then ''s'' = (1/''n'',&nbsp;''z'') must belong to ''D''. Choose ''r'' such that 1/(''n''&nbsp;+&nbsp;1) < ''r'' < 1/''n''. Since ''f''(''U'') does not intersect the ''x''-axis, the sets ''A'' = (&minus;&infin;, ''r'') &times; <math>\R</math> and ''B'' = (''r'', +&infin;) &times; <math>\R</math> will form a [[separated sets|separation]] on ''f''(''U''); contradicting the connectedness of ''f''(''U''). Therefore, ''f''<sup>&nbsp;&minus;1</sup>{''p''} is both open and closed in [0,&nbsp;1]. This is a contradiction.
* The comb space is [[Homotopy|homotopic]] to a point but does not admit a [[Retraction (topology)|strong deformation retract]] onto a point for every choice of basepoint that lies in the segment <math>\{0\} \times (0,1] </math>
